conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and check on how you’re feeling emotionally. To do that, I’ll use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days—no right or wrong answers, just whatever is true for you. Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me you’re in immediate danger. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause any time you need. Ready to start?

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*shifts in chair, eyes down for a moment*

Honestly... it's been pretty hard. My sister sent me this funny video the other day - normally I would've laughed so hard, but... I just kind of smiled a little and felt nothing. It's like the joy is muted or something. My husband tried to joke with me yesterday morning and I wanted to laugh for his sake, but it felt forced. I hate that I can't seem to find anything really funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… not really. I mean, I *want* to laugh, but it’s like there’s this heavy blanket over everything. Even when my mom tried to show me that same silly video she used to make me crack up at, I barely managed a smile. I keep thinking, “This should be funny,” but the laugh just doesn’t come.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*wrings hands in lap*

That’s… that’s been tough. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park, even just a quiet shower. Now I wake up and feel… flat. I still go through the motions, but it’s like I’m watching myself from outside. Yesterday my best friend texted about grabbing brunch next week and I texted back “sure,” but inside I felt nothing. I *want* to look forward to it, but the spark just isn’t there anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, eyes watering*

Yeah... I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn't nap and I kept thinking it was because I'm doing something wrong as a mom. When he cried for what felt like hours, I kept replaying everything in my head - maybe I ate something that upset him through my breastmilk, or I'm not holding him right, or... I don't know. My partner says I'm too hard on myself, but when the baby is fussy or I can't soothe him immediately, this voice in my head just says "you're failing him." Even when the diaper leaked through to the bedsheets at 3am, I apologized to my husband like it was my fault. I know rationally that babies cry and these things happen, but I can't stop feeling like I'm letting everyone down.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*presses palms together tightly*

Yes… pretty much every day. It’s like my mind won’t shut off. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly I’m sure he’s going to choke—even though he’s latched fine. Or I’ll picture him rolling off the changing table when I just turned away for a second. Last night I checked the monitor five times because I was terrified he’d stopped breathing. There’s no real reason, but the fear just barges in and I can’t talk myself down for a while. It’s exhausting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*nods quickly, voice trembling*

Yes… it hits out of nowhere. A couple nights ago I was rocking the baby in the quiet living room and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t breathe—like something awful was about to happen, even though we were both safe. I had to put him in the crib for a minute and sit on the floor with my head between my knees so I wouldn’t pass out. There was no trigger; it just surged up and left me shaking. It’s scary feeling that out of control for no reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales shakily, shoulders sagging*

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Yesterday the baby spit up on the last clean onesie right after I’d started a load of laundry, and I just sat on the floor and cried. It’s like every tiny task—folding a blanket, warming a bottle—adds another brick and I can’t keep up. I make lists, but then I stare at them and feel paralyzed. I know it’s just dishes and diapers, not rocket science, yet I keep thinking, “I can’t do this,” even though I somehow muddle through each hour.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*pulls cardigan tighter around shoulders*

That’s been happening a lot. I finally get the baby down, finish the bottles, crawl into bed—and then my brain just won’t quit. I lie there replaying everything I might have done wrong, worrying about SIDS, worrying he’ll wake up the second I fall asleep. Some nights it takes two or three hours to drift off, and then I jolt awake at every tiny sound. Even when I do sleep, it’s light and restless. By morning I feel like I never really rested at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

*eyes glaze, voice drops*

Pretty much every day, yeah. It’s like there’s this gray fog that won’t lift. I’ll be holding the baby and tears just start leaking out—no warning, no reason. Sometimes I stare at the wall while he nurses and feel… hollow. I keep thinking I should be grateful—he’s healthy, I’m not alone—but the sadness just sits on my chest. I hate that I can’t shake it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*voice cracks, fingers twisting the edge of her sleeve*

Yeah… it happens. A couple times this week I just broke down—once when the baby finally fell asleep on me and I couldn’t move, and another time when my mom texted to ask how I was doing. I tried to type “fine” and the tears started before I could hit send. It feels like there’s this pressure behind my eyes all the time, and any tiny thing can push it over the edge. I hate crying because it scares my husband, but I can’t always stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*looks away, jaw trembling*

…once or twice. Nothing planned—just these quick flashes when everything feels too heavy. Like, I’ll be washing bottles at 2 a.m. and think, “What if I just kept my head under the water?” It’s gone as fast as it comes, and I’d never do anything; I couldn’t leave my baby. But the fact the idea even pops in terrifies me. I haven’t told anyone that.

You have shared that the joy and anticipation that used to color your days now feel muted, replaced by a heavy fog of sadness, self-blame, and constant worry. Simple tasks feel overwhelming, humor and excitement are distant, and even sleep brings little rest. Fleeting thoughts of escape have surfaced, though you remain devoted to your baby and would never act on them.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes complete inability to laugh despite recognizing humor, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes anhedonia: loss of anticipation for previously enjoyable activities, emotional flatness, and absence of positive feelings.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states she blames herself "most of the time," with multiple vivid examples of excessive self-blame over normal infant behaviors, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, irrational fears that are persistent and hard to control, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden intense panic with physical symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, shaking) occurring without trigger, matching 'Yes, quite a lot</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling completely overwhelmed daily, unable to manage routine tasks, and experiencing paralysis and tears—semantically matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling asleep for hours, restless light sleep, and no sense of rest, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, daily sadness with uncontrollable crying and emotional emptiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by minor events, consistent with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 27 (range 0-30) places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating high probability of major <med>peripartum depression</med> with comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. You describe nearly every day over the past week as filled with pervasive sadness, inability to enjoy anything, disproportionate self-blame, middle- and late-night insomnia, feeling unable to cope, and sudden panic. <quote>I just feel hollow</quote> and <quote>I can't talk myself down</quote> mirror <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for major depressive episode with peripartum onset. Item 10 endorsement, though low frequency, signals safety risk requiring immediate clinical attention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to review results and discuss treatment options
2. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you until professional support is in place; share your safety thoughts with them so you are not alone
3. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or your local emergency services if urges to self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
4. Consider evidence-based treatments: individual <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>, support groups, and/or antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding
5. Plan small, achievable daily goals-one shower, one 5-minute outdoor walk-and accept help with night feeds or household tasks to protect sleep
6. Continue monitoring mood; keep a brief log of anxiety spikes, crying episodes, and any further self-harm thoughts to review with your clinician
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ___

Patient: 4–6 wks post-delivery, breastfeeding, partner at home.

Self-report on EPDS-10 equivalent:

A. Mood / Enjoyment  
- Persistent anhedonia (loss of humor, anticipatory pleasure)  
- Daily sad/hollow mood, frequent tearfulness without precipitant  

B. Cognition / Self-appraisal  
- Pronounced inappropriate guilt (“failing baby,” “letting everyone down”)  
- Ruminative self-blame re infant care  

C. Anxiety spectrum  
- Daily free-floating worry (SIDS, choking, minor mishaps)  
- Discrete nocturnal panic episode (palpitations, breathlessness, fear of passing out)  

D. Neuro-vegetative  
- Initial and maintenance insomnia linked to racing worries  
- Overwhelmed by routine tasks (“drowning in small stuff”)  

E. Safety  
- Passive self-harm ideation fleeting but present (“what if I kept my head under water”); denies intent or plan; protective of infant  

Summary: Screening reveals high likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; passive suicidal ideation present. Safety risk identified; patient requires immediate risk assessment and referral for psychiatric evaluation/treatment.
